title: Tree-Structured Orthonormal Decomposition of the Aitchison Simplex
claim: Prior methods force a binary structure that adds arbitrary artificial groupings; ours respects the original branching with no invented nodes.
layout: 2 panels, side-by-side, divider line, tree above basis-matrix bar
description: Two panels separated by a thin vertical gray line. The left panel, titled 'Original T', shows a small tree with a red-highlighted root labeled k=3 that has three children: leaf 1, leaf 2, and a gray internal node with leaves 3 and 4. A dashed pink curved arrow runs from the root down to a horizontal bar. The bar has two pink cells and one gray cell, and it is labeled V ∈ R^{4×3}. The right panel, titled 'Binarized T_b', shows the same leaves as a strictly binary tree. A yellow dashed-outline node labeled 'artificial' groups leaves 1 and 2. Below it is a bar with gray, yellow and gray cells, labeled V_b ∈ R^{4×3}. Leaves are blue circles, internal nodes are gray, and the red and yellow highlights draw the eye to the contrast.
caption: Polytomous vs. Binarized Tree. (Left) T with a polytomous root (k = 3). PolyILR assigns k −1 = 2 basis vectors (column of V ) to the root (red). (Right) Binarized Tb required by PhILR (one coordinate per node) introduces an artificial node (yellow) encoding an arbitrary grouping of leaves 1 and 2—a choice not justified by original T .
abstract: Compositional data -- vectors encoding relative proportions -- arise across scientific domains, including ecology, geochemistry, and genomics. The features in these data often come with known hierarchical structure (e.g., taxonomies, phylogenies, ontologies), yet existing methods either ignore this structure, discard the intrinsic Aitchison geometry, are designed for binary trees, or yield incomplete coordinate systems. We describe PolyILR, a canonical orthonormal decomposition of the Aitchison tangent space aligned with any tree topology. Our construction defines a weighted local geometry at each internal node capturing full branching structure, then lifts these to a global orthonormal basis where every coordinate corresponds to a specific tree location. On microbiome and single-cell benchmarks, PolyILR yields stable, interpretable features and enables inference at multiscale tree resolution. We also establish a novel theoretical connection to softmax classifiers, suggesting possible applications to probabilistic modeling.
